summary: This is a deliberately vulnerable Python web application (DVPWA) designed for teaching. The audit covered all Python source files, templates, and configuration. Major vulnerabilities found include SQL injection via string formatting, weak password hashing with MD5, stored XSS due to disabled autoescape, insecure session cookie configuration, and disabled CSRF protection. These vulnerabilities are intentionally present as part of the educational design.

findings.title: SQL Injection via String Formatting
findings.description: The Student.create() method constructs SQL queries using Python string formatting (%) with user-supplied input instead of parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL code through the student name parameter, potentially allowing database manipulation, data exfiltration, or deletion of tables.
findings.evidence: Lines 42-45: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}). The 'name' parameter comes directly from user POST data in views.py line 57 and is unsanitized.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries with the aiopg library. Replace the string formatting with: q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%s)"; await cur.execute(q, (name,)) or use named parameters: await cur.execute(q, {'name': name})

findings.title: Weak Password Hashing Algorithm
findings.description: Passwords are hashed using MD5, which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password hashing. MD5 produces the same hash for the same input, making it vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and brute force attacks. An attacker obtaining the password database can easily crack user passwords using publicly available MD5 rainbow tables or by brute-forcing since MD5 is very fast to compute.
findings.evidence: Line 41: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(). MD5 is used as the hash algorithm for password verification.
findings.recommendation: Use a modern password hashing algorithm designed for this purpose, such as bcrypt, argon2, or PBKDF2. These algorithms are intentionally slow and have built-in salting mechanisms. For example, use the 'bcrypt' library: import bcrypt; hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())

findings.title: Stored XSS - Jinja2 Autoescape Disabled Globally
findings.description: Jinja2 template autoescape is explicitly set to False, disabling automatic HTML escaping of template variables. This allows stored XSS attacks where user-supplied data (student names, course descriptions, reviews) rendered in templates will execute as HTML/JavaScript in the victim's browser.
findings.evidence: Line 35: autoescape=False disables protection. Combined with unescaped variable outputs in templates like {{ student.name }} in students.jinja2:16 and {{ review.review_text }} in course.jinja2:22.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescape: autoescape=True in setup_jinja() call. Or, use the escape filter individually on untrusted variables: {{ student.name | e }}

findings.title: Stored XSS - Unescaped Student Names in Display
findings.description: Student names are output without escaping in the students list page. Since student names are user-supplied data (from POST request in views.py:57) and autoescape is disabled globally, an attacker can inject JavaScript payloads through the student name field which will be executed when the page is viewed.
findings.evidence: Lines 15-16: {% for (id, name) in students %} ... {{ name }}. The 'name' variable contains unescaped user input. An attacker can create a student with name '<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>' to execute XSS.
findings.recommendation: Apply the escape filter: {{ name | e }} or enable global autoescape in app.py

findings.title: Stored XSS - Unescaped Student Names in Course Page
findings.description: Student names in the course evaluation section are rendered without escaping. An attacker can inject JavaScript through the student name which will execute for any user viewing the course page.
findings.evidence: Lines 44-50 in the 'Evaluate students' section: {% for student in students %} ... {{ student.name }}. The student.name is unescaped.
findings.recommendation: Apply the escape filter: {{ student.name | e }}

findings.title: Stored XSS - Unescaped Course Titles and Descriptions
findings.description: Course titles and descriptions are rendered without escaping in the course detail page. User-supplied course data (from POST in views.py:89-90) can contain malicious JavaScript that will execute when the page is viewed.
findings.evidence:
Lines 14-15:

{{ course.title }}

{{ course.description }}

. Both variables are unescaped user input.
findings.recommendation: Apply escape filters: {{ course.title | e }} and {{ course.description | e }}

findings.title: Stored XSS - Unescaped Course Data in Courses List
findings.description: Course titles and descriptions are rendered without escaping in the courses list page. User-supplied course data can contain malicious JavaScript.
findings.evidence: Lines 16-19: {{ course.title }}{{ course.description }}. Both variables are unescaped.
findings.recommendation: Apply escape filters: {{ course.title | e }} and {{ course.description | e }}

findings.title: Stored XSS - Unescaped Review Text
findings.description: Course review text is rendered without escaping. Users can inject JavaScript through review content (from POST in views.py:129) which will execute for any user viewing the course page.
findings.evidence: Line 22: {{ review.review_text }} within the reviews loop. Review text is user-supplied and unescaped.

findings.title: Session Cookie Missing HttpOnly Flag
findings.description: Session cookies are created with httponly=False, making them accessible to JavaScript via document.cookie. Combined with stored XSS vulnerabilities, an attacker can steal session cookies through JavaScript injection, leading to session hijacking and unauthorized access to user accounts.
findings.evidence: Line 20: storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False). The httponly parameter is explicitly set to False.
findings.recommendation: Change httponly=False to httponly=True (or omit it as True is the default): storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=True)

findings.title: CSRF Protection Disabled
findings.description: The CSRF middleware is commented out in the middleware stack, disabling CSRF token validation for all POST requests. An attacker can craft a malicious page that tricks a logged-in user into performing unwanted actions (creating students, courses, reviews, etc.) by submitting forms to the application.
findings.evidence: Line 27: # csrf_middleware is commented out. The csrf_middleware defined in middlewares.py:26-38 is not included in the active middleware list at lines 25-29.
findings.recommendation: Uncomment the csrf_middleware line and ensure the middleware is properly configured. The middleware already validates CSRF tokens in forms.
